origin: A convention of continuity editing, standard since Hollywood's studio era.
meaning: Keep the camera on one side of an imaginary line between characters so their screen positions and directions stay consistent.
use: In a two-person scene, decide which side of the line you're on; if you cross it, do it deliberately, at a moment of disorientation or reversal.

origin: Michel Chion, The Voice in Cinema (1982), borrowing 'acousmatic' from the composer Pierre Schaeffer.
meaning: A character who is heard but not seen, whose voice seems to be everywhere and know everything, until showing the body (de-acousmatization) strips the power away.
use: Keep a threatening or powerful figure offscreen as a voice for as long as you can, and treat the moment we finally see them as a deliberate turn.

origin: The five-act rule goes back to Horace's Ars Poetica (late 1st century BCE), was revived by Renaissance critics and analysed by Freytag (1863); the three-act screen model was popularized by Syd Field in Screenplay (1979).
myth: Three-act structure is often credited to Aristotle, but he described a whole with a beginning, middle and end, not acts.
meaning: A large movement of a story, usually ending on a turn that changes the situation. Theorists disagree about how many acts a story has; in television an act is also the stretch between commercial breaks.
use: Write one sentence for each act that names the situation at its end; if two acts end in the same situation, they are really one. Then check that every act ends on a turn the audience can feel, not just on a page count.

origin: Newsroom practice; Alden Whitman at The New York Times (from the mid-1960s) made a point of interviewing subjects for their own.
meaning: An obituary written and kept on file before the subject dies, updated over the years.
use: Report an advance like a profile while the subject can still talk, then keep the first paragraph ready for the news.

origin: Susan Sontag, in the essay "Against Interpretation" (1964), collected in Against Interpretation (1966).
meaning: Sontag's argument that hunting for hidden meanings tames art, and that critics should attend to form and to what a work does to the senses. Her essay ends by calling for "an erotics of art" in place of a hermeneutics.
use: When you workshop a piece, describe what you experienced moment by moment before anyone says what it means. If a scene only works once it's explained, the meaning is sitting on top of the form instead of inside it.

origin: Murray Smith, Engaging Characters (1995).
meaning: How the narration attaches us to a character: spatio-temporal attachment (following them) and subjective access (knowing their thoughts and feelings). It is not moral approval.
use: Decide whose movements the story follows and whose mind it opens. To keep us with a difficult character, raise alignment while letting allegiance fall.

origin: Comedy production slang; Jesse Armstrong described the practice on Succession (2018–2023) in interviews around the 2023 finale.
meaning: An alternative version of a line, supplied so actors can try it in a different take.
use: For the line you're least sure of, write two alts, one funnier and one truer, and read all three aloud before choosing.

origin: Aristotle, Poetics (c. 335 BCE), ch. 11.
meaning: Recognition: a change from ignorance to knowledge, ideally about who someone really is, and best when it coincides with a reversal.
use: Plan your biggest reveal so it reverses what the character (and audience) believed and forces a new action. In journalism, place the turning fact where it overturns the reader's assumption.

origin: Gérard Genette introduced these terms in Narrative Discourse (Discours du récit, 1972; English 1980), as part of his analysis of narrative order.
meaning: Analepsis is a jump back in time (a flashback); prolepsis is a jump forward (a flash-forward). Genette calls any departure from chronological order an anachrony.
use: Before using a flashback, ask what question in the present it answers; place it right after the audience has started to wonder. A prolepsis (showing the ending first) trades the question "what happens?" for "how did it come to this?", which is often stronger for true stories whose outcome is known.

origin: Roland Barthes, "Rhetoric of the Image" (1964).
meaning: The way a caption or text fixes one of an image's many possible meanings.
use: Write captions as carefully as the story, and check they say only what you know about the image.

origin: Ira Glass, in the video series Ira Glass on Storytelling, which circulated online from the mid-2000s.
meaning: Glass's two building blocks of a radio story: the anecdote, a sequence of actions that raises questions and pulls the listener forward, and the moment of reflection, where someone says what it means.
use: Mark each paragraph or tape segment as A (action) or R (reflection) and check that they alternate; a long run of either one loses people. If you can't find a reflection, ask your subject "Why does this matter to you?" on tape.

origin: The word is old (it appears in English in the 18th century); Dostoevsky's narrator in Notes from Underground (1864) calls himself one. Modern usage covers any protagonist who lacks conventional heroic virtues.
meaning: A protagonist we follow without approving of: selfish, criminal or cruel, but compelling.
use: Decide what holds us instead of likability: fascination, competence, or people around them who are worse. Use at least one, from the first scene.

origin: Robert McKee, Story (1997), which sets archplot against miniplot and antiplot as the corners of his "story triangle".
meaning: The classic design: an active protagonist pursues a goal through mostly external conflict, in continuous time and a causal chain, to a closed ending. Miniplot minimizes these features (internal conflict, open endings); antiplot breaks them (coincidence, fractured time).
use: Decide which corner your story belongs to before judging it by archplot rules. If you choose miniplot, the audience still needs something to track, such as a slowly changing relationship or a question of understanding.

origin: Noël Carroll, The Philosophy of Horror, or Paradoxes of the Heart (1990).
meaning: The emotion horror aims at: fear mixed with disgust at a monster that is both dangerous and impure, breaking our categories (dead yet alive, human yet animal).
use: Make your monster violate a category, not just threaten, and build the plot around discovering and proving it exists.

origin: A convention of Elizabethan and Restoration drama, in which a character speaks briefly to the audience while others on stage are assumed not to hear.
meaning: A short remark to the audience in the middle of a scene, unheard by the other characters.
use: Use asides to open a gap between what a character shows the others and what they tell us; a character who never stops making them may be hiding.

origin: A long-standing television writers' term for the secondary storyline (with A, B and C stories); Blake Snyder made "B Story" a named beat in Save the Cat! (2005). No single originator is known.
meaning: A second storyline, usually smaller and often a relationship, that runs alongside the main plot and comments on it.
use: Make the B story carry the theme the A story can't say out loud: often it's where the protagonist learns what they need to win the A story. Test it by cutting it; if the climax loses nothing, the B story isn't connected yet.

origin: In acting, from Stanislavski's "bits" (units) of a role; in screenwriting, defined by Robert McKee in Story (1997) as an exchange of action and reaction. The word's origin is uncertain.
myth: The story that American actors got "beat" from Russian teachers pronouncing "bit" with an accent is charming but unproven.
meaning: The smallest unit of change in a scene: a shift in what a character is doing to get what they want. In outlines, "beat" also loosely means any story event.
use: Go through a scene and mark every place a character changes tactic; each mark starts a new beat. If a page has no new beat, the characters are repeating themselves and you can cut or compress.

origin: Popularized by Blake Snyder's "Blake Snyder Beat Sheet" in Save the Cat! (2005); the general industry term for a list of story beats is older and of unclear origin.
meaning: A one- or two-page list of a story's main events in order, used to plan or pitch before writing pages. Snyder's version names fifteen beats with page targets.
use: Write a beat sheet before your next draft, one line per beat, and read only the verbs: if they don't build, the draft won't either. Treat page targets as a diagnostic after drafting, not a mould.

origin: From Alison Bechdel's comic strip Dykes to Watch Out For, in the 1985 strip "The Rule"; Bechdel credits the idea to her friend Liz Wallace and prefers the name Bechdel-Wallace test.
meaning: A quick check for whether a film has at least two women who talk to each other about something other than a man. It measures a pattern across many films, not the quality of one.
use: Run it on your own script and on the ensemble around your protagonist: if your secondary characters only exist in relation to the lead, give two of them a scene with a want of their own. Use it as a prompt to look, not as a pass/fail grade.

origin: Coined by Karl Morgenstern in lectures at the University of Dorpat (1819–20); popularized by Wilhelm Dilthey from 1870. The model is Goethe's Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship (1795–96).
myth: Often credited to Dilthey, who popularized it; Morgenstern coined it half a century earlier.
meaning: A story of a young person's formation over time, educated by experience, ending in accommodation with society or rupture from it.
use: Write the protagonist's answer to "who am I, and where do I belong?" at the start and at the end; the story is the road between the two.

origin: The term humour noir was popularized by André Breton's Anthologie de l'humour noir (1940).
meaning: Comedy that laughs at death, war, cruelty or madness, as in Dr. Strangelove (1964).
use: Make the laughter look harder at the subject, not away from it; the joke should sharpen the horror.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! (2005), one of his 'laws of screenplay physics'.
meaning: Piling one clever idea on another: a premise with two unrelated hooks becomes a gimmick.
use: Say your premise aloud. If it needs 'and also' to describe the hook, cut one of them.

origin: Stage lighting term; the "blackout sketch" of vaudeville and revue took its name from the sudden darkness that ends it.
meaning: Cutting all stage light at once: theatre's hard cut, as opposed to a slow fade.
use: Decide the last image before darkness; use a blackout for a punch, a fade to let a moment linger.

origin: Theatre term, now standard in film and television; of uncertain origin.
meaning: The plan for where performers stand and move in each moment, and the picture it makes.
use: Draw the stage or frame and mark positions at the start, turn and end of a scene; let one move toward or away from someone be an action.

origin: Northrop Frye's term in Anatomy of Criticism (1957), for a stock role going back to Greek New Comedy.
meaning: The figure, often a father or rival, who stands in the way of the young hero's desire; comedy tends to convert and include them at the end rather than destroy them.
use: Give your comic obstacle real authority, and decide whether the ending welcomes them in or shuts them out.

origin: Lajos Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946).
meaning: Egri's three dimensions of character: physiology (the body), sociology (class, work, family, beliefs) and psychology (the temperament and drives that grow from the other two).
use: Write a few lines under each heading for a character who feels thin, then check whether their want comes from their sociology and their need from their psychology.

origin: Popularized in creative nonfiction teaching by Brenda Miller, notably in Tell It Slant (2003, with Suzanne Paola); Jo Ann Beard's "The Fourth State of Matter" (The New Yorker, 1996) is a much-taught example.
meaning: A personal essay that twists together several threads, often a personal story, a research subject and an image, without explaining how they connect.
use: Write each thread separately, then interleave short sections and let echoes between them carry the meaning.

origin: As old as multi-plot novels such as Anna Karenina and films such as Griffith's Intolerance (1916). In narrative nonfiction, books like Erik Larson's The Devil in the White City (2003) and Isabel Wilkerson's The Warmth of Other Suns (2010) made it a familiar form.
meaning: Two or more stories told in alternation, so that each changes how the reader understands the others.
use: Give each strand ground the others can't cover, switch at moments of tension, and decide whether the strands converge or work by contrast.

origin: Ursula K. Le Guin, "The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction" (written 1986, published in Dancing at the Edge of the World, 1989), drawing on Elizabeth Fisher's Women's Creation.
meaning: Le Guin's proposal that a story can be a container that holds many things in relation, rather than a spear-shaped arc of conflict and triumph.
use: Try organizing a piece around a gathering place or an object that collects lives (a kitchen, a ward, a bag) and let relationships, not a single conflict, carry the reader. Give the reader a reason to keep going anyway: curiosity, accumulation, a question.

origin: Aristotle, Poetics (c. 335 BCE), ch. 6, where tragedy brings about the catharsis of pity and fear.
meaning: The release or transformation of emotion an audience experiences through tragedy. Aristotle never explains it fully, and scholars still debate whether it means purging, purifying or clarifying.
use: Ask what your audience should feel at the end and whether the story has earned it: pity requires that we understand the character, fear that we see ourselves in them. If the ending feels manipulative, you've asked for emotion the earlier scenes didn't build.

origin: From August Strindberg's chamber plays (1907), written for his Intimate Theatre in Stockholm after the model of chamber music; the German Kammerspielfilm of the 1920s took up the idea, and the term is often applied to Ingmar Bergman's films of the early 1960s, which he likened to chamber music.
meaning: A drama with a small cast, few locations and little plot, where the action is close pressure between a handful of people.
use: Cut to the fewest characters who pull against each other and one location, so pressure builds instead of leaking into new settings.

origin: A long-standing screenwriting and workshop term with no single originator; K. M. Weiland's Creating Character Arcs (2016) popularized the positive, negative (or disillusionment) and flat arcs.
meaning: The path of inner change a character travels over a story. In a positive arc they learn their need; in a negative arc they refuse it or learn the wrong lesson; in a flat arc they already hold the truth and change others.
use: Name which arc each lead is on, then find the scene where it turns. If a lead is on a flat arc, make sure the people around them change instead.

origin: A convention of screenplay format: the first time a character appears, the name is in capitals, often with an age, followed by a short description. No single originator.
meaning: A character's first appearance, and in a script, the description line that comes with it.
use: Write essence and attitude, not an inventory of looks, and follow it at once with an action only this character would do.

origin: John Truby, The Anatomy of Story (2007).
meaning: Truby's idea that characters should be designed together, each defined by contrast with the others and each a different answer to the hero's moral problem. Four-corner opposition sets a hero, a main opponent and two secondary opponents against each other.
use: Write the value each character stands for. If two characters stand for the same thing, merge or cut one.

origin: Based on Anton Chekhov's remarks in letters and conversation, including an 1889 letter to Alexander Lazarev (Gruzinsky) and a reminiscence by Ilia Gurlyand published in 1904.
myth: Chekhov stated the rule several ways and didn't always follow it; the popular version, "every detail must pay off", is a simplification.
meaning: The principle of economy: don't plant an element the audience will notice unless it is going to matter.
use: Underline every object, skill or fact you draw attention to in Act One and check that each is used later; cut or quiet the ones that aren't. In nonfiction, the same test applies to details in the lede.

origin: Italian for "light-dark", a term from Renaissance and Baroque painting (Caravaggio is the painter most associated with it), carried into film through German Expressionism and film noir.
meaning: Strong contrast between light and shadow, used to model forms and create drama.
use: Use it where you want something hidden or a face only half readable; a reveal can be as simple as a light coming on.

origin: The word is recorded from the early 1930s in film-serial slang; it is often traced to Thomas Hardy's A Pair of Blue Eyes (serialized 1872–73), where a character literally hangs from a cliff, but no link to the word has been shown.
meaning: An episode or chapter ending that leaves a character in danger or a question open, to make the audience come back.
use: End an episode on a new question, not just on a moment of peril: a revelation that changes what the audience thought the story was about lasts longer than a threat. Then pay it off promptly next time, or audiences learn to distrust your endings.

origin: From the Greek klimax ("ladder"), a rhetorical figure of rising intensity; Freytag's Höhepunkt (1863) was rendered "climax" in English, and the word is now used by nearly every structural theory.
meaning: The decisive confrontation or action where the story's central question is answered. Freytag put it at the centre of the play; modern screen models put it near the end.
use: State your story's central question in one line, then check that the climax answers it through the protagonist's own choice or action. If someone else solves the problem, move the decisive act back to your protagonist.

origin: Close views appear in British films around 1900 (G. A. Smith) and in The Great Train Robbery (1903).
myth: Often credited to D. W. Griffith, who used close-ups for emotion within stories but didn't invent them.
meaning: A shot that fills the frame with a face or object, isolating it for attention and emotion.
use: Save your closest images for your most important moments, so the cut-in itself tells the audience this matters.

origin: A television term for a scene before the opening titles; its first use is unknown.
meaning: A short opening scene that plays before the credits, designed to hook the viewer immediately. Also called a teaser.
use: Open with the most intriguing moment you can show without explanation, then cut to titles before answering it. A good test: could someone who switched on mid-scene still be curious?

origin: A long-standing practice in film design; no single originator.
meaning: A colour given a meaning that builds each time it returns, as distinct from a film's overall palette, like the red coat in Schindler's List.
use: Choose one colour for one meaning, plant it early, repeat it sparingly, and pay it off at a turning point.

origin: An old practice, named by critics; the Porter scene in Macbeth (Act 2, Scene 3) is the classic example.
meaning: A comic scene or character placed inside a serious work to release tension, often heightening the darkness around it.
use: Put the joke right after the worst moment, and let it echo the horror rather than ignore it.

origin: Jon Franklin, Writing for Story (1986).
meaning: Franklin's core of a true story: a complication, a problem that matters to a sympathetic person, and a resolution, a change that person brings about, ideally through insight.
use: Before reporting a narrative, try to state your story as one complication and one resolution in a few words each, in Franklin's spirit. If you can't, you may have a subject rather than a story, and an explanatory piece may serve it better.

origin: A long-standing practice in fiction, drama and some journalism; no originator. It became a central ethics issue in the debates over the New Journalism in the 1970s and 1980s.
meaning: A single character built from several real people. Common and accepted in fiction and dramatization; in journalism, unacknowledged composites are generally considered a breach of the reader's trust.
use: In journalism, don't use them; if you must for privacy, say so plainly in the text. In a fact-based play or film, disclose it in a note and keep each composite's key actions true to something that really happened.

origin: A fixed role in French classical tragedy, as with Oenone in Racine's Phèdre (1677); the device is much older.
meaning: A character the protagonist tells the truth to, which lets the audience hear their thoughts without a soliloquy or voice-over.
use: Give your confidant an agenda of their own, as Oenone has, so the confessions become scenes rather than exposition.

origin: Jonathan Franzen, "Mr. Difficult", The New Yorker (2002).
meaning: Two views of fiction: in the Status model a novel is art whose worth doesn't depend on readers' pleasure; in the Contract model it's an agreement in which the writer owes the reader something for their effort.
use: For any difficult stretch of your work, list what you ask of the audience and what they get back. If the second list is empty, the contract is broken.

origin: Robert McKee, Story (1997).
meaning: The story's meaning in a single sentence, naming a value and the cause of its final state, as shown by the climax.
use: Write one sentence: "[Value] wins/loses because [cause]." Then check that your climax demonstrates exactly that, and that the opposing idea gets its strongest case somewhere earlier.

origin: John G. Cawelti, 'The Concept of Formula in the Study of Popular Literature' (1969) and Adventure, Mystery, and Romance (1976).
meaning: Conventions are the familiar elements writer and audience both know in advance; inventions are the new elements a writer brings. Conventions give security, inventions surprise.
use: List the conventions your genre's audience expects, decide which to honour, and name the one invention that makes your story yours.

origin: A teaching distinction in this course for the two ways strands of a braid relate, not a term from one source.
meaning: In convergence, strands head toward a meeting the audience waits for; in contrast, they never meet and their meaning comes from comparison.
use: Decide which you're writing early, and signal it, so readers don't wait for a collision that never comes.

origin: From the Greek krisis ("decision"); used by many theorists, and defined by Robert McKee in Story (1997) as the protagonist's dilemma before the climax; Janet Burroway's Writing Fiction (1982) uses conflict, crisis and resolution.
meaning: The point of maximum pressure, where the protagonist must make a hard choice and the outcome is still open.
use: Make the crisis a genuine dilemma, two goods or two evils, so the choice reveals character. If your protagonist's choice is obvious, raise the cost of the right option.

origin: Earlier films such as Pathé's A Narrow Escape (1908) used it; D. W. Griffith developed and popularized it from The Lonely Villa (1909) to Intolerance (1916).
myth: Often said to be Griffith's invention; he refined it but didn't originate it.
meaning: Alternating between two or more lines of action, usually simultaneous, to build suspense, irony or comparison.
use: Cross-cut when the meaning lies in the relation between two events: a rescue racing a threat, a ceremony and a crime, two characters converging.

origin: As a story beat, Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! (2005), paired with "All Is Lost"; the phrase itself comes from the 16th-century Spanish poet St John of the Cross.
meaning: The low point after the protagonist's biggest defeat, when they sit with the loss before finding the way forward.
use: Give the protagonist a moment to absorb the defeat, ideally with an image of what they've lost, before the solution arrives. Keep it short on screen; on stage or in prose it can be where the real change happens.

origin: Roland Barthes, "The Death of the Author", first published in English in Aspen magazine (1967), then in French (1968).
meaning: Barthes's argument that a text's meaning is made by the reader, not settled by the author's intentions or biography.
use: When you get workshop feedback, listen to what readers actually took from the page rather than defending what you meant. If several readers miss your intention, change the text, not the reader.

origin: Made famous by cinematographer Gregg Toland in Citizen Kane (1941).
meaning: Keeping foreground, middle ground and background sharp at once, so several actions can matter in one frame.
use: Stage two related actions in one frame, near and far, and let the audience discover the connection instead of cutting to it.

origin: Viktor Shklovsky, "Art as Device" (1917); the Russian word ostranenie is his coinage.
meaning: Making the familiar strange, so that the reader sees it freshly instead of recognizing it automatically.
use: Describe a familiar thing as if seeing it for the first time, through a child, a foreigner or an animal, as Tolstoy does. In journalism, open on the routine detail an insider has stopped noticing.

origin: An old stage technique; Molière keeps Tartuffe offstage until Act 3 of Tartuffe (1669), and The Third Man (1949) withholds Harry Lime for about an hour.
meaning: Keeping an important character offstage while others talk about them, so their first appearance answers a question the audience has been asking.
use: Have the characters who discuss the absent one disagree about them. Then make the first line or gesture confirm or overturn the talk.

origin: French for "untying", a term from French neoclassical dramatic criticism that echoes Aristotle's lysis (unraveling) in the Poetics.
meaning: The final unravelling after the climax, where the consequences are shown and loose ends are tied up.
use: Keep it as short as the audience allows: show the one image or exchange that proves how things have changed, then stop. If you need several scenes to explain the ending, the climax hasn't done its job.

origin: Latin for "god from the machine", after the crane that lowered gods onto the Greek stage; Aristotle criticized such endings in the Poetics (ch. 15) and Horace warned against them in the Ars Poetica.
meaning: An ending in which an outside force suddenly solves the problem, rather than the plot's own logic.
use: Check that whatever resolves your climax was set up earlier and is driven by the protagonist's choice. If luck must play a role, Pixar's version of the rule applies: coincidence can get characters into trouble, not out of it.

origin: Diegesis is Greek for narration; Étienne Souriau's filmology group revived it for the story world in the early 1950s, Gérard Genette used it in narratology (1972), and textbooks such as Bordwell and Thompson's Film Art (1979) made the sound terms standard.
meaning: Diegetic sound comes from the story world and the characters could hear it; non-diegetic sound, like score or voice-over, is heard only by the audience.
use: Mark every sound in a scene D or N. Where you want the audience pulled into the characters' present, use diegetic sound, or reveal that apparent score was coming from a radio all along.

origin: Ancient on stage (the chorus, the Shakespearean soliloquy and aside); on screen it runs from Alfie (1966) and Ferris Bueller's Day Off (1986) to Fleabag (2016–2019), which made it the backbone of a series.
meaning: A character speaks or looks straight at the audience, acknowledging that they're being watched.
use: Decide what the audience is to the speaker (confidant, jury, accomplice) and set the rules early; then make breaking those rules a turn in the story.

origin: James Baldwin, "The Creative Process" (1962), written for the anthology Creative America.
meaning: Baldwin's name for the artist's role: from a cultivated state of being alone, the artist tells a society what it would rather not know, which is why societies have always battled the artist.
use: Ask what truth your story tells that its audience would prefer to avoid, and whether you have softened it to keep the peace.

origin: As old as Greek tragedy, where three speaking actors shared all the roles; a standard practice in theatre ever since.
meaning: One actor playing two or more roles in a production, for economy or to make a point, as when Mr Darling and Captain Hook are played by the same actor in Peter Pan.
use: When cutting a cast to size, look for pairs of roles that comment on each other, and double those.

origin: An ancient technique; the concept was influentially discussed by Connop Thirlwall in "On the Irony of Sophocles" (1833), and "dramatic irony" became a standard term later in the 19th century.
meaning: When the audience knows something a character doesn't, so every action carries a second meaning.
use: Tell the audience the secret early and let the character walk toward it; then write the scene in which they find out. In nonfiction, the reader knowing the outcome turns a subject's confident statements into suspense.

origin: A widely used teaching term (also "central dramatic question"); no single originator. Frank Daniel's related "main tension" is taught in Paul Gulino's Screenwriting: The Sequence Approach (2004).
meaning: The yes-or-no question that holds the audience's attention: will she get out? Who did it? The climax answers it.
use: Write your story's question in one line ending in a question mark; if you can't, the audience won't know what to watch for. Then check each sequence against it: does it make the answer more uncertain?

origin: Georges Polti's unit of analysis in The Thirty-Six Dramatic Situations (1895).
meaning: A configuration of roles and forces that produces conflict, such as a persecutor, a suppliant and a power whose decision is in doubt; the core of a plot rather than its whole shape.
use: When a scene has no tension, ask which situation it dramatizes and whether all its roles are present.

origin: A recurring move in 19th-century slave narratives, where narrators stopped short of the worst events; named and challenged by Toni Morrison in "The Site of Memory" (1987).
meaning: A deliberate silence in a historical account, shaped by what its original audience could bear or would accept.
use: Read every source for where it stops short and ask why; that silence may be where your story is.

origin: As old as film itself; no single originator. Ingmar Bergman's opening nightmare in Wild Strawberries (1957) is one of the most imitated examples.
meaning: A passage showing a character's dream, which can state a story's fears or theme in images before the plot does.
use: Use a dream only if it tells us something the waking story can't, and make its images concrete (a clock with no hands, a coffin in the road) rather than vaguely surreal.

origin: Associated with German Expressionist film and used throughout The Third Man (1949).
myth: The name is usually explained as a corruption of 'Deutsch', but that origin is hard to document.
meaning: A shot with the camera tilted so the horizon isn't level, suggesting unease, madness or a world out of joint.
use: Use sparingly, at the moment the story's world tips off balance; constant use stops registering.

origin: Charles Baxter, "Dysfunctional Narratives: or, 'Mistakes Were Made'", in Burning Down the House (1997).
meaning: Baxter's term for stories in which nobody takes responsibility: things happen to a passive protagonist, and the climax is a recognition of grievance rather than a choice.
use: Look for the moment where your protagonist could have acted and check whether they do. If your story is about something done to someone, give them at least one decision that matters, even if it fails.

origin: Gérard Genette named it among the speeds of narrative in Narrative Discourse (1972; English 1980); in film it's simply a cut that skips time.
meaning: A gap in the telling where story time passes but nothing is narrated; the audience fills it in.
use: Skip whatever the audience can infer, and plant one clue after the gap (a new haircut, a different flat) so they catch up without exposition.

origin: Used in computational studies of fiction, notably Matthew Jockers's Syuzhet tool (2015) and Andrew Reagan and colleagues' "The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes" (EPJ Data Science, 2016).
meaning: The rise and fall of emotional tone through a text, measured by scoring the happiness or sadness of its words in a moving window.
use: Treat it as a rough rhythm check, not a plot map: word mood can't see irony or contrast.

origin: Michel Chion, Audio-Vision (1990; English 1994).
meaning: Empathetic music expresses the feeling of the scene; anempathetic music carries on indifferent to it, which often intensifies the audience's response.
use: For each cue, name which it is. Try playing a cruel or tragic moment against a cheerful or neutral piece, and see whether the indifference hurts more.

origin: Hayden White, Metahistory (1973); Paul Ricœur developed a related idea (mise en intrigue) in Time and Narrative (1983–85).
meaning: The process of turning a sequence of events into a story of a particular kind, such as tragedy, comedy, romance or satire. White argued historians do this too, so the shape is chosen, not found.
use: Before writing up a true story, ask what genre you're casting it in (tragedy? redemption?) and try drafting the lede in a different one. If the facts fit both equally well, the shape is your choice and you owe the reader awareness of it.

origin: From the French for 'together'; on stage Chekhov is the model, and television dramas like The Wire (2002–2008) and Succession (2018–2023) made it their home.
meaning: A story with no single protagonist, whose meaning lies in the pattern of its characters.
use: Give the whole cast one shared want and a different weapon each, rotate whose story each episode or scene is, and bring them together where they have to choose sides.

origin: Developed in 1920s Germany by Erwin Piscator and Bertolt Brecht; Brecht set out its contrast with "dramatic" theatre in his notes to Rise and Fall of the City of Mahagonny (1930).
meaning: A theatre that narrates rather than immerses, interrupting the action with songs, titles and direct address so the audience thinks about the social causes of what they see.
use: Interrupt your own story at the moment of highest emotion with a title, a song or a direct address that asks the audience a question. Use it where you want judgment, not empathy.

origin: In its literary sense, from James Joyce, in Stephen Hero (written c. 1904–06, published 1944), borrowing a religious term.
meaning: A sudden moment of insight in which a character, or the reader, sees the truth of a situation.
use: Earn the epiphany with a concrete trigger: an object, a line, a gesture, not a summary of what the character realizes. End close to it, before the character explains it.

origin: Aristotle's Poetics, which calls episodic plots, where events follow one another without probability or necessity, the worst kind.
meaning: A plot of self-contained incidents that could be reordered without loss.
use: Test by shuffling two middle episodes; if nothing breaks, add a clock, a hidden question or a changing relationship underneath.

origin: An old newsroom form (the backgrounder), made a brand by sites such as Vox in the 2010s.
meaning: A piece that starts from the reader's question, answers it briefly, then adds layers of context and uncertainty.
use: Write the reader's question at the top of your draft and make sure the third paragraph has answered it.

origin: An old term of rhetoric and dramatic criticism with no single originator; it is the first part of Freytag's five-part scheme (1863), which he called the introduction.
meaning: The background information the audience needs: who these people are, what happened before, what the rules are.
use: Deliver it when the audience wants it, ideally in a scene where someone has a reason to say or hide it. Test each line of backstory: if the audience isn't asking yet, delay it.

origin: A convention of continuity editing standardized in Hollywood's studio era.
meaning: A cut from a character looking off-screen to a shot of what they're looking at, positioned so the look and its object line up.
use: Write what each character looks at in key moments; a look followed by its object is the simplest way to put the audience in someone's head.

origin: Russian Formalists in the 1920s, especially Viktor Shklovsky and Boris Tomashevsky.
meaning: The fabula is the events in their chronological order; the syuzhet is the order and manner in which they are told.
use: Write your events in chronological order on one list and in telling order on another; every difference is a choice you should be able to justify. Try one experiment: start with the event that raises the biggest question.

origin: Toni Morrison's distinction in "The Site of Memory" (1987): facts can exist without human intelligence, but truth cannot.
meaning: Facts are events and data that stand whether or not anyone thinks about them; truth is what they meant to the people inside them, which only a mind can make.
use: In fiction, invented facts can carry truth. In journalism, keep facts sacred, then ask whether the accurate piece is also true.

origin: An English textbook label for the downward slope of Freytag's pyramid, which Freytag (1863) called the "return or fall".
meaning: The events after the climax, leading to the ending. In Freytag's tragedy it is half the play; in modern films it is short.
use: Keep the falling action proportionate: on screen, show consequences quickly; on stage, use it for a last flicker of suspense, as Freytag recommended. If it drags, cut until only the change is shown.

origin: From a French word for stuffing, used for comic interludes in medieval drama; perfected by Georges Feydeau in 1890s–1900s Paris.
meaning: Comedy as accelerating machinery: flat characters driven by one appetite or fear, secrets, doors, and people who must not meet.
use: Get every secret into one space by the end of the first act, then let the pressure rise until everything collides.

aka: Mythic, romantic, high mimetic, low mimetic, ironic
origin: Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (1957), first essay.
meaning: A ranking of fiction by the hero's power of action relative to us and their world, from a god (mythic) down to someone weaker than ourselves (ironic).
use: Decide whether your protagonist is above, level with or below the audience, and keep what they can do consistent with it.

origin: Coined by the French critic Nino Frank in 1946, after Paris saw a batch of wartime Hollywood crime films; spread by Raymond Borde and Étienne Chaumeton's Panorama du film noir américain (1955).
myth: Hollywood's makers didn't call their films noir; the label came later, and critics still debate whether it's a genre or a style.
meaning: Dark crime films of the 1940s and 1950s, and their heirs: a flawed protagonist, desire, a night city and a trap closing.
use: Let the audience sense doom early, even reveal the ending, and make the pleasure watching how the trap closes.

origin: The list goes back to the "circumstances" of classical rhetoric; it became newsroom doctrine in American journalism teaching in the early 20th century. Kipling's "six honest serving-men" (Just So Stories, 1902) is often quoted.
meaning: Who, what, when, where, why (and how): the questions a basic news report must answer.
use: Check your first two paragraphs against the list; anything missing should be there unless you've chosen to delay it. Then ask which W is the news, and lead with that one.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! Strikes Back (2009).
meaning: Snyder's breakdown of the Finale beat into five steps: Gathering the Team, Executing the Plan, the High Tower Surprise, Dig Deep Down, and the Execution of the New Plan.
use: If your climax is one long fight that simply works, let the first plan fail at a surprise, force the hero to find something inside, and finish with a new plan built on it.

origin: E. M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel (1927).
meaning: Flat characters are built around a single idea or quality; round characters are complex. Forster's test of a round character is whether it is "capable of surprising in a convincing way".
use: Pick your three main characters and write one thing each does that would surprise the reader but makes sense in hindsight. Keep minor characters flat on purpose: they are efficient and often funny.

origin: Gérard Genette, Narrative Discourse (1972), separating "who sees?" from "who speaks?".
meaning: The perspective through which events are perceived, as distinct from the voice telling them.
use: Identify whose perceptions shape each scene; if it shifts mid-scene without purpose, choose one. For suspense, focalize through someone who knows less than the reader.

origin: From the jeweller's foil, a thin metal leaf set behind a gem to make it shine; Shakespeare puns on it in Hamlet ("I'll be your foil, Laertes").
meaning: A character whose likeness to another, in situation or goal, makes their differences stand out.
use: Give your hero someone facing the same problem who chooses differently. If no one does, the hero's choices have nothing to be measured against.

origin: A general literary term with no single originator; Egri lists foreshadowing among his tools in The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946).
meaning: A hint early in a story of what will come later.
use: Plant the hint where the audience is looking at something else, so it registers without announcing itself. Test on a reader: they should not predict the ending, but should recognize it once it arrives.

aka: Mythos of spring, summer, autumn, winter
origin: Northrop Frye, Anatomy of Criticism (1957), third essay; taken into history-writing by Hayden White's Metahistory (1973).
meaning: Frye's four basic plot movements, each tied to a season: comedy (spring), romance (summer), tragedy (autumn), irony and satire (winter), arranged on a circle so each shades into its neighbours.
use: Name your story's season in one word, then decide on purpose where it leans toward a neighbouring one.

origin: The idea is usually traced to Denis Diderot, Discourse on Dramatic Poetry (1758), who advised actors to imagine a wall separating them from the audience; the phrase spread with 19th-century realist theatre.
meaning: The imaginary wall between the stage and the audience. "Breaking the fourth wall" means addressing the audience directly.
use: Decide your contract early: if you break the wall, do it in the first ten minutes so the audience accepts it. Use direct address to share information the characters can't, or to make the audience complicit.

origin: An ancient device: the One Thousand and One Nights and Boccaccio's Decameron (c. 1353) set their tales inside a storytelling occasion.
meaning: An outer story that contains and organizes an inner one, such as the depositions in The Social Network (2010) that frame the founding of Facebook.
use: If a true or sprawling story lacks shape, find a present-tense situation (a trial, an interview, a reunion) that gives the past a reason to be told and a question to answer.

origin: Practised by Jane Austen and Gustave Flaubert; the French term style (or discours) indirect libre was named by the linguist Charles Bally in 1912.
meaning: Third-person narration that takes on a character's thoughts and voice without quotation marks or "she thought".
use: Take a passage of reported thought and remove the tags, letting the narration use the character's own words and judgments. In nonfiction, only do this with thoughts your source told you, and say so somewhere in the piece.

origin: Gustav Freytag, Die Technik des Dramas (1863), with a diagram of the five-act tragedy; the five textbook labels (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, dénouement) are later simplifications.
myth: The school version, with a late climax, describes a different shape; Freytag's own pyramid is symmetrical with the climax at the centre.
meaning: A model of tragedy rising through an exciting force to a climax at the centre, then falling through a tragic force to the catastrophe.
use: Draw the shape of your own story and see where its peak actually falls; most modern stories peak late, not in the middle. Use Freytag's "force of final suspense" to lift a sagging ending.

origin: Vladimir Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928).
meaning: The 31 basic actions that recur, always in the same order, across a corpus of Russian wonder tales, distributed among seven roles (spheres of action) such as villain, donor and false hero.
use: List your plot's main actions as functions (lack, departure, test, gift, struggle, return) and see which roles your characters play; one character can play several. Useful for spotting a missing donor or test.

origin: Robert McKee, Story (1997).
meaning: The difference between what a character expects to happen when they act and what actually happens.
use: At each turning point, write what the character expected and what they got; if those match, there's no gap and the scene may not turn. Widen the gap to raise surprise and the cost of the next action.

origin: Bertolt Brecht, from the late 1920s, adapting an older German word.
meaning: A gesture or attitude that reveals the social relations between characters, not just individual feeling.
use: For a key scene, find one physical action that shows the power relation (who pays, who waits, who stands). Make it visible and repeatable so the audience can read it.

origin: John Truby, The Anatomy of Story (2007).
meaning: An event from the past that still haunts the protagonist and helps explain their weakness.
use: Give your protagonist one specific past event that causes their present weakness, and reveal it late rather than up front. If your story is driven entirely by the ghost, check that present choices still matter.

origin: Konstantin Stanislavski, who took the phrase from Pushkin's writing on drama; it became central to his system in An Actor Prepares (English, 1936).
meaning: Everything the actor and the character must take as true: time, place, history, relationships and the events of the play.
use: Write down the given circumstances of a scene before you write it: what happened in the hour before? What do they want next? The scene will carry the pressure even if none of it is mentioned.

origin: Northrop Frye, "The Argument of Comedy" (1948), developed in Anatomy of Criticism (1957).
meaning: The forest or countryside in Shakespeare's comedies, like the Forest of Arden, where characters escape a harsh society, are transformed, and return to renew it.
use: Give your comedy an escape place with different rules, and make sure the characters bring something back.

origin: Aristotle, Poetics (c. 335 BCE), ch. 13.
myth: "Tragic flaw" is a later moralizing gloss; Aristotle means a mistake of judgment or knowledge, not necessarily a defect of character.
meaning: The error or mistake that brings about a tragic hero's fall. Better translated as "error" than "tragic flaw".
use: Build your catastrophe out of a mistake your character makes in good faith, from ignorance or misjudgment. It hits harder than one caused by villainy.

origin: Roland Barthes, S/Z (1970), one of his five codes alongside the proairetic (actions), semic, symbolic and cultural codes.
meaning: Everything in a text that raises, delays and finally answers a question or enigma: the code of mystery.
use: List the questions your opening raises, then mark where each is answered; Barthes's lesson is that the delays (snares, partial answers, red herrings) are where suspense lives. Never leave the reader with no open question.

origin: Joseph Campbell described the monomyth in The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), taking the word from James Joyce's Finnegans Wake; Christopher Vogler's Hollywood memo (1985) and The Writer's Journey (1992) turned it into twelve stages for screenwriters.
myth: Campbell was describing myths, not prescribing screenplays; the twelve-stage version writers use is Vogler's.
meaning: A pattern of departure, initiation and return in which a hero leaves the ordinary world, faces trials, and comes back changed with something to share.
use: Use it as a checklist for what your middle may be missing (a mentor, a threshold, an ordeal) rather than a template to fill. Ask what your hero brings back to the ordinary world; if nothing, the return has no point.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! Strikes Back (2009), the third step of his five-point finale.
meaning: The twist in the finale that breaks the hero's plan: they reach the tower and the princess isn't there. It works like a second catalyst.
use: Find the moment in your climax where the plan is going well, and break it with something the hero (and audience) didn't see coming but that was set up earlier.

origin: Hollywood studio lighting terms, named for the balance between the key light and the fill light.
meaning: High-key lighting fills the frame with soft, even light and few shadows; low-key lighting lets one main source dominate, with deep shadows and strong contrast, as in film noir.
use: Name the light source in a scene description (a single lamp, noon glare) when the mood matters; low-key for secrecy and danger, high-key for openness and comedy.

origin: Musical-theatre trade term for a number early in the show.
meaning: A song in which the protagonist states the desire that drives the musical, like 'Wouldn't It Be Loverly' or 'Part of Your World'.
use: Put your hero's want into one early number, specific enough that we'll know when they get it.

origin: Ernest Hemingway, Death in the Afternoon (1932), comparing good prose to an iceberg with most of its mass below the surface.
meaning: The idea that what a writer knows and leaves out can strengthen a story, if the omission is deliberate.
use: Write the backstory or the feeling in full in your notes, then cut it from the draft and see what the scene implies on its own. Omit only what you know well; leaving out what you haven't worked out just leaves a hole.

origin: Michael Hauge, Writing Screenplays That Sell (1988; revised 2011), which lists ways to create it: sympathy through undeserved misfortune, jeopardy, likability, humor, and power or skill.
meaning: The audience stepping into a character's shoes and experiencing the story through them, so that what happens to the character matters to us.
use: Label the moments in your hero's first scenes with Hauge's tools. If you can't find at least two, the audience may not attach to them in time.

origin: A linguistics term usually credited to Bernard Bloch (1948).
meaning: The speech habits peculiar to one person: vocabulary, rhythm, sentence length, pet phrases and what they never say.
use: Cover the names on a page of dialogue. If you can't tell who's speaking, give each character a distinctive habit of speech.

origin: A screenwriting maxim of uncertain origin; it is often linked to William Goldman's advice to enter scenes as late as possible, in Adventures in the Screen Trade (1983), but no source has been found for the exact phrase.
meaning: Start each scene as late as you can and leave as soon as its point has landed.
use: Cover the first and last few lines of every scene; if the scene still works, cut them. Arrive after the greetings and leave before the goodbyes.

origin: Horace, Ars Poetica (late 1st century BCE), praising Homer for hurrying the reader "into the middle of things".
meaning: Starting a story in the middle of the action, filling in earlier events later.
use: Open at the first moment of real pressure, then ask what backstory the audience actually needs and when. Don't start mid-action just for energy: the reader has to care about who is in danger.

origin: Popularized for screenwriters by Robert McKee in Story (1997); the idea corresponds to Freytag's "exciting force" (das erregende Moment, 1863). The exact phrase's first use is uncertain.
meaning: The event that upsets the balance of the protagonist's life and launches the story's central conflict.
use: Find the moment your protagonist's normal can't continue and check it's an event, not a mood; then make sure the protagonist reacts to it on the page. If it happens too late, the audience may lose patience before the story starts.

origin: The distinction between direct and indirect action in Chekhov's plays was drawn by David Magarshack in Chekhov the Dramatist (1952).
meaning: Major events happen offstage or between acts, while the onstage scenes show people talking around them.
use: Try moving a big event offstage and writing the scene before or after it; the audience reads it in the characters' behaviour. Works especially well for grief, money and love.

origin: Walter Benjamin, "The Storyteller" (1936).
meaning: Benjamin's contrast between information, which is only valuable while new and comes already explained, and story, which keeps its power because it leaves the reader free to interpret.
use: Remove one explanation from your piece and let the facts stand; the reader's own interpretation will stay with them longer. Useful in features where the urge is to tell the reader what to think.

origin: Aaron Sorkin's name for the core of drama, taught in his MasterClass (2016) and many interviews; he credits Aristotle's Poetics, though the phrase is his, and it echoes the actor's language of objectives from Stanislavski.
myth: It's sometimes presented as a term from the Poetics; Aristotle never uses it.
meaning: Somebody wants something, and something stands in the way of getting it. Without both, a scene is just talk.
use: Write 'wants ___, blocked by ___' at the top of each scene for every character. If you can't fill both blanks, strengthen the want or the obstacle, or cut the scene.

origin: Silent cinema used intertitles for dialogue and narration; sound films kept them for chapter headings, as in The Worst Person in the World (2021), with its prologue, twelve titled chapters and epilogue.
meaning: Text shown full-screen between shots or sections, naming a chapter, a time or a place.
use: Use chapter cards when a story jumps through time: they make the gaps honest, and their wording can give the film a voice of its own.

origin: An old practice with no single originator; Lynn Nottage's Ruined (2009) and Sweat (2017) are leading examples. Distinct from verbatim theatre, which uses only real people's words.
meaning: Plays whose characters and plots are invented but grow out of long interviews with real people.
use: Use interviews for texture (jobs, routines, jokes, local words) and build a fictional plot; tell interviewees you're writing fiction, and keep composites honest.

origin: Developed in American newspapers in the second half of the 19th century; the familiar story that Civil War telegraph lines forced it is not well supported.
myth: The telegraph origin story is popular but historians, including David T. Z. Mindich (1998), find the form spread later and for other reasons.
meaning: A news structure that puts the most important facts first and the rest in descending order of importance.
use: Write your lede to stand alone, then rank every remaining paragraph by importance; editors should be able to cut from the bottom. Before filing, check what got ranked last: it's often context or people who were affected.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! (2005).
meaning: Snyder's test that a hero's drive should be one anyone, even a caveman, would understand: survival, protecting loved ones, love, fear of death.
use: Write your hero's goal in one line, then ask what basic need it stands for. If you can't find one, deepen the goal.

origin: A rhythmic principle from Japanese court music (gagaku), developed for Noh by Zeami Motokiyo in his treatises of the early 1400s.
meaning: Three phases, a slow beginning (jo), a breaking or development (ha) and a rapid conclusion (kyū), applying to a whole programme, a play, a scene or a gesture.
use: Shape a scene, an episode or a feature so it accelerates: let the opening breathe and let the end come fast. Check the rhythm at several scales, not just the whole piece.

origin: Made famous by Jean-Luc Godard's Breathless (1960).
meaning: A cut that removes a piece of a continuous shot, so the image visibly skips forward in time.
use: Use jump cuts for restlessness, impatience or compressed time within a single situation; in prose, the equivalent is dropping the connective tissue between moments.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! (2005), who credited it to Steven Spielberg.
meaning: Once news crews arrive in a story, it stops feeling private and real, unless the story is about the press.
use: Before you cut to a news report to raise the stakes, try showing the effect on one character instead.

origin: Seymour Chatman, Story and Discourse (1978), adapting Roland Barthes's "nuclei" and "catalysers" (1966).
meaning: Kernels are the events that open choices and can't be removed without changing the story; satellites fill out, elaborate or delay.
use: Mark every scene K or S; you can cut satellites for length, but not kernels. If a draft has too many kernels it races; too many satellites, it drifts.

origin: Newsroom jargon of uncertain origin.
meaning: The ending of a feature story, often a quotation, image or detail that circles back to the opening or leaves a final note.
use: Save your best quote or image for the kicker, not the middle. Test it: if it would work at the end of any story on the subject, find something more specific.

origin: A four-part structure from Chinese poetic composition (qǐ chéng zhuǎn hé), long used in Japanese and Korean writing; it became famous in English as "plot without conflict" in the 2010s.
myth: It is often presented as a conflict-free Eastern alternative to Western drama, but conflict often appears within it and it is mostly taught as a composition pattern.
meaning: Introduction, development, a twist that brings in something apparently unrelated, and a conclusion that reconciles them.
use: Take two unrelated situations and write a piece where the meaning comes from their juxtaposition rather than a struggle. Put most of your effort into the ending, which has to make the twist resonate.

origin: Lev Kuleshov's Moscow film workshop, around 1918–1921, best known through Vsevolod Pudovkin's account; demonstrated by Hitchcock in a 1964 CBC interview with Fletcher Markle.
myth: The original footage is lost and accounts vary; modern replications show a real but weaker and less consistent effect than the legend.
meaning: Viewers read the meaning of a shot, especially a face, from the shots around it, so the same expression seems to show different emotions in different contexts.
use: Before writing an emotion onto a face, write the image the character is reacting to; test a key moment by imagining two different things the character could be looking at.

origin: German, "artist novel"; a branch of the bildungsroman. James Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) is the standard example.
meaning: A story of an artist's growth, usually ending with a break from home, family or nation in order to make art.
use: Make the art the thing the hero must choose over belonging, and let the ending cost them something.

origin: A newsroom respelling of "lead", recorded from the mid-20th century; the usual explanation, that it avoided confusion with the metal strips used in typesetting, is plausible but unproven.
meaning: The opening of a news story, usually its first sentence or paragraph.
use: Write the lede last, and ask what a reader needs to know if they read only that sentence. For a feature, an anecdotal lede must point toward the nut graf; otherwise it's a detour.

origin: Associated with Richard Wagner's operas, especially the Ring cycle; the word was popularized by commentators, notably Hans von Wolzogen in the 1870s.
myth: Often said to be Wagner's own term, but he rarely used it.
meaning: A short musical idea attached to a character, place or idea that returns and develops as the story does.
use: If you use a theme, let it change as the character changes, and bring it back softly when they're absent so the music carries memory.

origin: Toni Morrison's term, in her talk "The Site of Memory", published in William Zinsser's anthology Inventing the Truth (1987).
meaning: Starting from real remains (documents, fragments, memories), going to the 'site' and reconstructing the world those remains imply, imagining only what fits the evidence.
use: Before inventing, gather what survives and list what it implies; let your invention fill gaps without contradicting the record.

origin: Championed by critic André Bazin in the 1940s–50s; famous examples include the Copacabana shot in Goodfellas (1990).
meaning: A single shot held for an unusually long time without a cut, often with the camera moving.
use: Use it when continuous time and space are the meaning, such as entering a world or a pressure that can't be escaped; every beat inside it must hold.

origin: Popularized by Alfred Hitchcock, whose 1939 Columbia University lecture is the earliest recorded use; Hitchcock's collaborators credit the screenwriter Angus MacPhail with the term.
meaning: The object or goal the characters chase that matters to them but barely matters to the audience.
use: If your plot revolves around a secret object, keep the focus on what the chase does to the people. Spend as little time explaining the MacGuffin as the audience will tolerate.

origin: Laura Mulvey, "Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema", Screen (1975).
meaning: The way classical cinema positions the viewer to look at women through a heterosexual male perspective, making them objects of looking rather than subjects of the story.
use: In each scene, ask whose eyes the camera or the prose is using and who is being looked at. If a female character exists to be seen, give her a want and a point of view of her own.

origin: Kurt Vonnegut's name for the shape; the 2016 University of Vermont study by Andrew Reagan and colleagues kept the name for one of its six emotional arcs.
meaning: Someone gets into trouble, gets out of it, and ends up better off than before: a fall followed by a rise.
use: If your second act is one long climb, try a double hole: let the hero climb out, then fall again before the final rise.

origin: Coined by the critic Nathan Rabin in a 2007 A.V. Club review of Elizabethtown; he later said he regretted how widely and loosely it was used.
meaning: A quirky young woman who exists in a story mainly to teach a gloomy male hero to enjoy life, with no inner life or goals of her own.
use: Test any character who exists to change the hero: what do they want for themselves? If the answer is nothing, give them a want or rethink the role.

origin: A long-standing editing technique; the bone-to-spacecraft cut in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) is the most famous example.
meaning: A cut that joins two shots through a shared shape, movement or sound, making a connection between them.
use: End a scene on an image that rhymes with the next scene's opening image to link them in meaning or leap across time.

origin: Henri Bergson, Laughter (Le Rire, 1900).
meaning: Bergson's theory that we laugh when a person behaves like a machine, repeating, rigid or inattentive when life requires flexibility.
use: Give a comic character a rigid habit and then put them in a situation that demands they adapt. The more serious the situation, the funnier the rigidity.

origin: From Greek melos (song) and drama; Rousseau's Pygmalion (1770) and Pixerécourt's Cœlina (1800) in France, Holcroft's A Tale of Mystery (1802) in England. Theorized by Peter Brooks in The Melodramatic Imagination (1976).
myth: The heroine tied to the railway tracks is rarer than its fame suggests; in Augustin Daly's Under the Gaslight (1867) the heroine rescues a man from the tracks.
meaning: Drama of persecuted virtue and plain villainy, ending in a scene where virtue is recognized, originally with music cueing every emotion.
use: When you need moral stakes loud and clear, let characters say what they feel and give the turn a big recognition scene; use it knowingly.

origin: Tennessee Williams's description of The Glass Menagerie (1944) in its production notes.
meaning: A play presenting the past as a narrator remembers it, so staging can be non-realistic: dim light, music, magnified moments, a frame of the present.
use: Give your narrator a reason to remember now, and let what memory exaggerates or omits shape the staging.

origin: From Mentor in Homer's Odyssey, whose form Athena takes to advise Telemachus; the modern sense owes much to Fénelon's The Adventures of Telemachus (1699). Vogler lists it among his archetypes (1992).
meaning: A character who guides, trains or equips the hero, and who usually leaves or fails so the hero must act alone.
use: Decide when your mentor exits. If the mentor solves the final problem, the hero hasn't grown.

origin: The term was coined by the novelist and critic William H. Gass in his essay 'Philosophy and the Form of Fiction' (1970); the practice is much older, as in Don Quixote and Tristram Shandy.
meaning: Fiction that draws attention to its own making, as in Adaptation (2002), a film about the writer failing to write it.
use: Use self-awareness only when the making of the work is genuinely the subject; otherwise it's a wink that lets the writer avoid committing.

origin: Industry slang named after early Disney cartoons, whose music matched the action beat for beat.
meaning: Music that imitates the on-screen action note for note.
use: Use it deliberately in comedy and animation; in drama, if the music is describing what we can already see, cut it back.

origin: Syd Field, The Screenwriter's Workbook (1984), as a revision to his paradigm; Kristin Thompson and others find a similar central turning point in Hollywood films.
meaning: A turn halfway through that splits the second act and changes the direction of the story: a false victory, a false defeat or a new goal.
use: Find the halfway mark and ask what changes there; if nothing, write an event that raises the stakes or reverses what the protagonist believes. In a long feature, use a key discovery as the midpoint.

origin: André Gide borrowed the term from heraldry in his journal (1893) for a work that contains a small image of itself.
meaning: A story within a story that mirrors the whole, such as the play-within-the-play in Hamlet or the replica city inside the warehouse in Synecdoche, New York (2008).
use: If you nest a story inside yours, make it reflect the outer story's question, so each level comments on the other.

origin: French theatre term ("putting on stage"), taken into film criticism by the critics of Cahiers du cinéma in the 1950s; defined for students by David Bordwell and Kristin Thompson in Film Art: An Introduction (1979).
meaning: Everything placed in front of the camera or on the stage: setting, costume and makeup, lighting, and the staging of performers.
use: Before writing dialogue, decide the light, one colour, one telling object and where people stand, and put those that carry the conflict into the scene description.

origin: Bill Nichols, Representing Reality (1991), extended in Introduction to Documentary (2001).
meaning: Six ways documentaries address their audience: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive and performative.
use: Name the mode of your film or podcast, then decide whether to use another for one section, for instance switching from observational to reflexive when you face an ethical choice. Make the shift on purpose.

origin: Soviet filmmakers of the 1920s, especially Sergei Eisenstein (Battleship Potemkin, 1925) and Vsevolod Pudovkin; the Hollywood 'montage sequence' is a later, different use of the word.
meaning: In Soviet theory, the creation of meaning through the juxtaposition or collision of shots; in Hollywood usage, a sequence of short shots that compresses time.
use: Use a collision of two images to make a point without stating it; use a montage sequence for change the audience must accept quickly rather than live through.

origin: Peter Brooks, The Melodramatic Imagination (1976).
meaning: The hidden moral truths that melodrama drags into the open, making good and evil legible in a world without a guaranteed sacred order.
use: Ask what moral truth your scene is uncovering, and let it be seen in gesture, face and speech, not left to subtext.

origin: Arthur Quiller-Couch, in a 1914 Cambridge lecture "On Style", published in On the Art of Writing (1916).
myth: It is often credited to William Faulkner, Oscar Wilde or Stephen King, but it is Quiller-Couch's.
meaning: Cut the passages you love most if they serve your pleasure more than the piece.
use: In revision, mark the line you're proudest of and ask whether it serves the story or shows off; if the second, cut it and save it in a file. Quiller-Couch was warning against ornament, not every good sentence.

origin: Melanie Green and Timothy Brock (2000), building on Richard Gerrig's Experiencing Narrative Worlds (1993).
meaning: The experience of being absorbed into a story's world, which research associates with changes in readers' beliefs and attitudes.
use: Remove anything that pulls the reader out (an error, a jarring explanation) at the moment you most need them absorbed. Use concrete scene and a character to follow; abstract argument transports less.

origin: Broadcast newsroom jargon, short for "natural sound".
meaning: Sound recorded on location, such as footsteps, traffic, a crowd or a kettle, used to place the listener in a scene.
use: Let the recorder run before and after every interview; open a piece with a few seconds of real sound. Don't add or move sound from elsewhere without telling listeners.

origin: Industry term, from lowering a record player's needle onto an existing recording.
meaning: An existing song or recording placed in a film, as opposed to music composed for it.
use: Choose a song for what its lyrics, era and associations do to the scene, and decide whether it plays in the story world or over it.

origin: The comedy of Menander in Athens in the late fourth century BCE, adapted into Latin by Plautus and Terence.
meaning: Domestic comedy of young lovers, blocking fathers, clever servants, mistaken identities and lost children, ending in recognition and marriage; the ancestor of romantic comedy and the sitcom.
use: When your comedy needs an engine, give the lovers an obstacle with authority over them, and end with a recognition that brings the group together.

origin: Newsroom jargon associated with The Wall Street Journal's feature style from the 1970s; it was taught by William E. Blundell in The Art and Craft of Feature Writing (1988).
meaning: The paragraph near the top of a feature that tells the reader what the story is about and why it matters.
use: After your anecdotal lede, write a paragraph beginning "This matters because…" and then delete those words. If you can't write it, you haven't found the story yet.

origin: Konstantin Stanislavski's zadacha ("task"), translated as "objective" by Elizabeth Hapgood in An Actor Prepares (1936).
meaning: What a character is trying to do to another person in a given moment, best expressed as an active verb.
use: For each character in a scene, write "I want to [verb] you"; if the verbs don't clash, there's no conflict. Replace weak verbs like "talk to" with playable ones like "seduce" or "shame".

origin: Francisque Sarcey's scène à faire in 19th-century French theatre criticism; William Archer rendered it "obligatory scene" in Play-Making (1912).
meaning: The scene the audience has been led to expect and would feel cheated without.
use: List the scene your setup has promised (the confrontation, the discovery) and check you've written it, on stage, not reported. Surprise the audience with how it happens, not whether.

origin: Hollywood slang for overly direct dialogue; origin unknown.
meaning: Dialogue in which characters say exactly what they think and feel, with no subtext.
use: Find lines where a character states their emotion and rewrite them so they talk about something else while the feeling leaks through. If a character explains the theme, cut the line.

origin: The modern practice is usually dated to Allan Nevins's oral history office at Columbia University (1948); Studs Terkel's books, such as Hard Times (1970) and Working (1974), popularized it.
meaning: Recorded interviews in which people describe their own past, kept as an archive for later researchers.
use: Look for interviews your subjects gave others, especially ones recorded in confidence. They're often more candid than anything said to a reporter, but check how they were gathered and what was promised.

origin: Named as one of the seven basic plots by Christopher Booker (2004).
meaning: A hero confronts a deadly force threatening a community and destroys it, moving through Anticipation and Call, Dream, Frustration, Nightmare, and Thrilling Escape.
use: Let the hero feel equal to the threat (the Dream Stage) before the monster's real power shows.

origin: Fast overlapping exchanges were a hallmark of Howard Hawks's His Girl Friday (1940); Robert Altman developed multitrack recording to layer whole conversations, on California Split (1974) and Nashville (1975).
meaning: Dialogue in which characters talk over and interrupt each other, as in life, rather than waiting their turn.
use: In a crowded or heated scene, let two lines collide where a character can't wait. Mark in the script which line must be heard.

origin: John Ruskin, Modern Painters, volume 3 (1856), chapter "Of the Pathetic Fallacy".
myth: It's often treated as a technique Ruskin admired; he coined it as a criticism, of the false picture of nature that strong emotion produces.
meaning: Giving nature human feelings, especially weather or landscape that mirrors a character's mood. "Pathetic" means "of feeling".
use: Matching rain to grief is the easy choice; try weather that means different things to different characters, or that plays against the mood.

origin: Aristotle, Poetics (c. 335 BCE), ch. 11.
meaning: A reversal: an action produces the opposite of what was intended, turning the situation around.
use: Find a moment where a character's action backfires and make it the turn of your act. The strongest reversals come from the character's own effort, as in Oedipus.

origin: Murray Smith, in an essay on 'apparently perverse allegiances' that followed Engaging Characters.
meaning: Siding with a villain or criminal; Smith argues that many apparent cases are really fascination, or the result of surrounding the character with worse people.
use: If you want the audience with a dark character, know which tool you're using: worse enemies, access to their reasons, suspense, or charisma.

origin: From Spanish pícaro, rogue. Founded by the anonymous Lazarillo de Tormes (1554), made popular by Mateo Alemán's Guzmán de Alfarache (1599, 1604).
meaning: An episodic story, usually told in the first person, of a low-born rogue who survives by his wits through a series of masters or places, satirizing each, and changes little.
use: Use it when you want a tour of a society; give each episode a new target, and add an engine underneath if you need suspense.

origin: Syd Field, in work after Screenplay (1979), as part of his second-act scaffolding.
meaning: A smaller event in each half of the second act, reminding the audience of the central conflict.
use: Halfway between plot point I and the midpoint, put a scene that shows the antagonist's force; do the same after the midpoint. Use it to fight the second-act sag.

origin: Harold Pinter's plays from The Birthday Party (1958) on, which mark three dots, "Pause" and "Silence" in the text.
meaning: A scripted silence that carries meaning, usually a moment of pressure or a shift of power, rather than a gap in the talk.
use: Mark pauses only where something shifts between characters. If a pause doesn't change the scene, cut it.

origin: Syd Field, Screenplay (1979).
meaning: An event that hooks into the action and spins it in a new direction, ending Act I and Act II in Field's paradigm.
use: Find your two plot points and check each forces the protagonist into a new kind of action. If an act ends without one, the story is drifting.

origin: William Wallace Cook, Plotto (1928).
meaning: A vast cross-referenced system of plot fragments that can be chained into stories; a more elaborate cousin of Polti's list.
use: Use it, like Polti, to break a block, not to replace knowing your characters.

origin: Pamela Regis, A Natural History of the Romance Novel (2003), one of her eight essential elements of the romance novel.
meaning: The moment in a romance when union between the lovers seems impossible, often marked by images of death or despair.
use: Give your romance a real low point where the barrier seems to have won, so the recognition that follows earns the ending.

origin: A basic film convention; the subjective camera was tried for a whole film in Robert Montgomery's Lady in the Lake (1947).
meaning: A shot showing what a character sees, usually framed by a shot of them looking; pushed to extremes, the subjective camera makes the camera the character.
use: Use a brief point-of-view shot to make the audience share a discovery; avoid long stretches, which hide the face that builds sympathy.

origin: Mikhail Bakhtin, Problems of Dostoevsky's Art (1929; revised 1963).
meaning: A novel in which many independent voices and worldviews are given equal weight, without the author's voice settling the argument.
use: Give your antagonist's worldview its strongest possible speech. If the reader can tell which side you're on from the dialogue alone, try writing the other side better.

origin: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat! (2005).
meaning: Snyder's name for hiding exposition inside something entertaining, so the audience absorbs it while watching something else.
use: Find your most explanatory scene and stage it during an activity with its own tension or comedy: a chase, a meal going wrong, a job being done badly. If the scene would still be fun with the exposition muted, it works.

origin: A critical term from media and film criticism, in wide use since the 2000s; no clear originator. Lynn Nottage invoked the worry when discussing Sweat (Slate, 2016).
meaning: Work that displays poor people's hardship for the audience's pity or thrill rather than portraying them as full people.
use: Test every character in a story about hardship: do they have humor, knowledge and choices, or do they exist only to suffer?

origin: Lajos Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing (1946), which borrowed the word from logic and argument.
meaning: The proposition a play proves through its conflict and outcome, in the form "X leads to Y".
use: State your premise in three parts (character, conflict, conclusion) and check the ending actually proves it. Then ask if a stronger opponent would make the proof more convincing.
